episode_thesis: Mark Rzepczynski argues that the 2026 bond sell-off is a return to normal (nominal yield = real rate of about 2-2.5% + inflation of about 3% + a positive term premium, so about 5-5.5%), not an anomaly, and that investors should study the micro foundations and plumbing of markets (who trades, dealer intermediation capital, convenience yield, geo-economic fragmentation) rather than only price action. For trend following he draws three conclusions: fragmentation raises diversification across markets, stock-out risk makes market-specific crisis alpha in low-inventory, low-substitute commodities, and trend following has no alpha half-life, unlike crowded machine-learning strategies whose models converge.

speakers.name: Mark Rzepczynski
speakers.role: Systematic investor and researcher; co-host of the Systematic Investor series; trend-following and institutional-structure thinker
speakers.speaker_note: Auto-captions: 'Merlin' for Perry Mehrling, 'Ibbotson's book' etc. The ledger notes that in C08 he lists 1980s-90s upheavals while the host observes the industry starts crisis alpha with the tech bubble. In C12 he says the convenience yield 'may have disappeared' at the long end (not stated as fact). Recorded about Thursday 22 October 2026 (data as of Tuesday 20 October; upload 2026-10-27).

worldview_premises.premise: Asset prices follow earnings divided by the discount rate; stocks can rise while discount rates rise only because earnings growth exceeds the discount rate effect, and when earnings momentum stops the discount rate dominates.
worldview_premises.support: Textbook dividend-discount reasoning.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend followers do not need falling bond prices: the belief that trend following profits only when bonds rally reflected the 1981-2020 secular decline in yields; with rates back to normal bond markets are two-way and shorts can pay.
worldview_premises.support: Historical yield path, Niederhoffer's paper and JGB trends in the last 12 months.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend profitability depends on the institutional structure of a market: who trades (hedgers vs speculators, governments vs profit maximisers) shapes trend persistence; markets with more hedgers than speculators favour trend followers who take the other side.
worldview_premises.support: Experience across markets; 'new institutional structural' approach.

worldview_premises.premise: Market-level 'micro foundations' matter: agents, exchange rules and policy-induced profit-maximising behaviour shape price direction, and money moves through a global plumbing system (payment systems, dealer financing, shadow banking), so capital flows matter.
worldview_premises.support: Analogy to the Hall and Woodford Nobel and Perry Mehrling's money view.

worldview_premises.premise: Crisis alpha should be identified ex ante by environment, not measured after the fact: a shortage of bank and dealer intermediation capital makes dislocations more likely.
worldview_premises.support: His own and others' work on intermediation risk; no figures given.

worldview_premises.premise: Under uncertainty and scarce liquidity, investors scale in and out of positions gradually, and this staggered behaviour produces the dislocations that appear as trends.
worldview_premises.support: Stated as a fundamental belief.

worldview_premises.premise: Globalization rested on a dominant dollar and institutions (World Bank, IMF); trend followers should be agnostic about globalization and simply exploit the environment, and globalization may have followed the benign 1990s economy rather than caused it.
worldview_premises.support: Kindleberger hegemon argument.

worldview_premises.premise: Crises (concentrated dislocations) differ from upheavals (changes in market behaviour that create long trends, e.g. commodity supercycles caused by underinvestment); trend followers also profit from the 1980s-90s upheavals, which the industry ignores.
worldview_premises.support: List of 1980s-90s events (Plaza, S&L, 1987, ERM, Latin America, Tequila).

worldview_premises.premise: The fair nominal yield equals the real rate (about 2-2.5%, trend growth plus productivity) plus expected inflation (about 3%, since inflation has been above target for over six years) plus a term premium; so about 5-5.5% on long Treasuries is normal and near current levels.
worldview_premises.support: Back-of-envelope arithmetic with Atlanta Fed GDPNow above 3% and inflation above 3%.

worldview_premises.premise: A positive stock-bond covariance and higher bond volatility should raise the term premium, unlike the negative-correlation era of near-zero term premia.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from risk compensation.

worldview_premises.premise: Public debt keeps rising while private credit to GDP is controlled; governments are not running primary surpluses after recessions, and interest costs crowd out other spending (US, France, Japan), pressuring long-term yields; private debt markets also crowd out public ones.
worldview_premises.support: BIS credit-to-GDP early-warning indicator; budget interest shares (Japan a third).

worldview_premises.premise: The composition of bond buyers has changed: hedge funds (multi-strat pods) trade basis and are more sensitive to losses than central banks were under QE, so demand is more elastic and moves can be large both ways.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning about pod risk limits; 'my guess'.

worldview_premises.premise: The convenience yield of safe assets rises in crisis but shrinks as supply of safe debt increases; the Treasury long end may have lost it, leaving bills, and the dollar's reserve convenience is diminishing on the margin as central banks diversify.
worldview_premises.support: Supply-demand argument; reserve-manager behaviour and Rogoff reference.

worldview_premises.premise: Geo-economic fragmentation (tariffs, sanctions, capital controls) reduces cross-market correlation, raising diversification for trend following; less fragmentation raises correlation, so correlation matrices must reflect geoeconomics.
worldview_premises.support: Qualitative; no correlation data shown.

worldview_premises.premise: Commodity spikes come from stock-outs: low inventories lead to hoarding and parabolic moves, and the nonlinearity is greatest where substitutes are few (diesel, cocoa).
worldview_premises.support: Examples: European winter gas stocks below 5-year norms, cocoa, hurricane/blizzard grocery hoarding.

worldview_premises.premise: Machine learning alpha has a shortening half-life because everyone adopts the same techniques, taught in the same schools, so strategies crowd and funds must spend more on compute (Red Queen); trend following has no alpha half-life because it just waits for dislocations.
worldview_premises.support: Research he cites: survey over 90% of hedge funds use ML; 13F similarity increasing.

worldview_premises.premise: Asking several AI models the same question gives similar answers, so AI-derived signals risk common-model herding; that is fine for facts but unreliable for novel ideas.
worldview_premises.support: Own informal experiment with ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude.

mechanism_chains.topic: Bond sell-off as return to normal

steps.from: Two decades of near-zero and negative yields
steps.to: Investors form beliefs that low yields are normal and the sell-off abnormal

steps.from: Real rate = natural rate = trend growth plus productivity (about 2-2.5%)
steps.to: Floor on real yields above zero

steps.from: Inflation above 2% for over six years
steps.to: Expected inflation about 3%

steps.from: Positive stock-bond covariance and more volatile bonds
steps.to: Positive term premium

steps.from: Sum of real rate, expected inflation and term premium
steps.to: 5-5.5% on long Treasuries, close to current levels

mechanism_chains.evidence: Rule-of-thumb decomposition with GDPNow and inflation prints; no model or survey data.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Inflation falls back to 2% faster than he assumes, growth or productivity disappoints, or hedge fund basis-trade unwinds drive a large fall or rally.

mechanism_chains.topic: Fiscal pressure and loss of convenience yield

steps.from: No primary surpluses after recessions and rising interest costs
steps.to: Public debt-to-GDP keeps rising while private sectors clean up
steps.why: Deficits persist beyond the counter-cyclical need

steps.from: More Treasury supply
steps.to: The safe-asset convenience yield shrinks, especially at the long end

steps.from: Central banks diversify away from the dollar
steps.to: Dollar's reserve convenience diminished on the margin; multipolarity

steps.from: France under stress
steps.to: France no longer clearly a safe asset; periphery may be less risky than assumed
steps.why: Sovereign debt of large countries is tested

mechanism_chains.evidence: Illustrations from US, France and Japan; no quantified convenience yield series.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: He hedges: the dollar's dominance is not in jeopardy, only relatively diminished.

mechanism_chains.topic: Intermediation capital to dislocations to trends

steps.from: Dealers and banks are capital constrained (repo problems, balance sheet limits)
steps.to: They cannot warehouse risk
steps.why: Balance sheet limits for risky assets

steps.from: Sellers cannot find buyers except quickly and disorderly
steps.to: Dislocations in bonds and commodities; flight to safety

steps.from: Scarce liquidity and uncertainty
steps.to: Gradual scaling in and out, creating trends

mechanism_chains.evidence: Conceptual; refers to his own work on intermediation risk.

mechanism_chains.topic: Fragmentation to diversification for trend following

steps.from: Tariff wars, sanctions, capital controls and industrial policy
steps.to: Markets decouple; lower cross-market correlation

steps.from: Lower correlation among positions
steps.to: Trend followers can take more risk and perform well
steps.why: Divergent strategies benefit from decorrelation; reversal risk is lower

steps.from: Different delivery points and tariffs
steps.to: Same commodity diverges across locations (London vs New York)

mechanism_chains.evidence: Qualitative; host recalls divergent versus convergent strategy framing.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Fragmentation eases and correlations rise, reducing diversification.

steps.from: Inventories low versus norms (Europe winter gas)
steps.to: Fear of stock-out, hoarding before the shortage
steps.why: Users pay any price to avoid shutdown

steps.from: Few substitutes
steps.to: Nonlinear, parabolic price spikes

mechanism_chains.topic: Alpha crowding in machine learning versus trend following

steps.from: Over 90% of hedge funds use ML; quants trained in same schools use the same methods
steps.to: Convergent models and positions (13F similarity rising)

steps.from: Crowding
steps.to: Shorter alpha half-life and faster market adaptation; funds jump to the next model
steps.why: Alpha is crowded out of each strategy

steps.from: Trend following waits for dislocations
steps.to: No alpha half-life; the cost is waiting without higher returns

mechanism_chains.evidence: A survey and a 13F similarity study he cites without naming; no direct trend-following test.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Trend following itself becomes crowded; he accepts no returns during no-trend periods.

decision_process.practice: Study the micro foundations and institutional structure of each market (who trades, exchange rules, government involvement, hedger-speculator mix) to judge whether trends will persist.
decision_process.why: Composition of participants shapes trend persistence.

decision_process.practice: Identify the environment rather than measuring crisis alpha after the fact: monitor dealer and bank intermediation capital and flight-to-safety conditions.
decision_process.why: Shortage of intermediation capital raises dislocation risk.

decision_process.practice: Use correlation matrices that reflect geo-economic fragmentation; diversification and risk capacity rise when fragmentation lowers correlation.
Consider trading the same commodity in different locations (London and New York copper, cocoa, coffee) when tariffs and delivery points make them diverge.
Look for stock-out candidates: low inventories relative to history and few substitutes.
decision_process.why: Nonlinear spikes occur where substitutes are absent.

decision_process.practice: Use machine learning to capture trends but make sure the strategy outlasts alpha crowding; test what others are doing.
decision_process.why: ML techniques are public and crowding shortens alpha half-life.

decision_process.practice: Cross-check several AI models and compare similarities and differences; trust them for facts, not for novel ideas.
Be patient with markets that long frustrate trend followers (cocoa shorts, JGBs); time in trend following matters more than timing trend following.
decision_process.why: Long-frustrating markets later produce big trends.

speakers.evidence_style: Historical context and first principles (discount model, Fisher-type decomposition), references to academic work (Hall, Woodford, Mehrling, Kindleberger, BIS indicators) and studies he cites from memory; frequent analogies; little quantification of his own.

current_views.view: The bond sell-off is a return to normal, not an oddity; fair long Treasury yield about 5-5.5%, close to current.
current_views.reasoning: Real rate 2-2.5% plus expected inflation about 3% plus positive term premium.

current_views.view: Public debt trajectories and the changed composition of bond buyers (hedge fund basis trades) mean bond moves could be large either way.
current_views.reasoning: More elastic hedge fund demand than central banks under QE.

current_views.view: The convenience yield of long Treasuries may have disappeared and sits mostly in bills; the dollar's reserve role is diminished relatively, not eliminated.
current_views.reasoning: More issuance; central bank reserve diversification.

current_views.view: France is no longer clearly a safe asset and southern European bonds may be less risky than thought.
Gold fell back from above $5,000 earlier in 2026 to about $4,100, challenging its safe-haven reputation over the last six months.
Commodities may be entering another supercycle driven by underinvestment, with a grind higher until a 2007-08 style reversal.
Europe's winter inventories are below 5-year expectations, so a cold winter could create a stock-out and parabolic gas prices.
Equity gains are carried by earnings momentum; if it stops, the higher discount rate will dominate.
current_views.reasoning: Earnings divided by a discount rate that rises with yields.

current_views.view: Geo-economic fragmentation is increasing diversification across markets for trend followers.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host of Top Traders Unplugged; veteran hedge fund manager (trend following)
speakers.speaker_note: Host who states several views and data points of his own; the ledger notes that the 'industry starts crisis alpha with the tech bubble' observation in C08 is his, while Mark gives the list of 1980s-90s events.

worldview_premises.premise: A large country's sovereign debt being tested (French 10-year near 5%, a 24-year high, amid unrest) changes how investors view safe assets and is reminiscent of past euro-area crises.
worldview_premises.support: Yield levels and the 12-month change cited.

worldview_premises.premise: Equity gains are carried by earnings momentum while valuation multiples have contracted; buyback tailwinds are ending and new supply is rising, so the competition for capital is stiffer.
worldview_premises.support: FIMO versus FOMO; conversations while travelling; prominent warnings.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets that long frustrate trend followers (cocoa shorts, JGBs) later give big trends, so time in the market matters more than timing trend following.
worldview_premises.support: Cocoa 'widow trade', JGBs one of the best markets in 12 months, Quantica paper.

worldview_premises.premise: Low correlation between trend positions lets managers take more risk and perform well; when correlations rise they should reduce risk because reversal risk grows.
worldview_premises.support: Referencing Katy Kaminski's convergent/divergent framework.

worldview_premises.premise: Peak globalization with stable inflation and falling rates produced a quiet period for trend followers, with no big drawdowns but weak returns.
worldview_premises.support: Personal view ('simple view').

worldview_premises.premise: In major crises trend followers are first hurt (wrong side) and then profit strongly; 1982 to the late 1990s was also very strong for trend; crisis alpha studies start with the tech bubble.
worldview_premises.support: Recollection of the industry's history.

worldview_premises.premise: Ultra-long bonds issued near zero rates (Austria 100-year) lost about 80%, showing the duration risk of the abnormal low-rate period.
worldview_premises.support: Example cited.

speakers.evidence_style: Performance data, anecdotes from travel and conversations, and industry history.

current_views.view: Early Q4 2026 was soft for trend: strong demand for 20-year JGBs (about six times covered) pulled yields down and hurt fixed-income positions, while energy trends remained good.
Trend barometer at 40 (lower end of neutral); CTA index about -1% in October but about +14% YTD; trend followers ran roughly level with equities and well ahead of bonds.
France's yields near 5% and unrest show sovereign stress that may persist.
He doubts that higher valuations justified by earnings can last forever.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Fair-yield arithmetic uses round numbers (real 2-2.5%, inflation 3%, term premium unspecified) and concludes that 5-5.5% is close to current levels; the term premium is not quantified, so the conclusion is loose.
Internal tension: the convenience yield is said to be eroding at the long end, yet the dollar's role is 'not in jeopardy'; and he says 'the dollar regime is breaking' in the same passage.
The convenience yield claim is hedged ('may have disappeared', 'may be one reason'); the ledger notes the speaker was less certain than the first reading.

Machine-learning crowding evidence (over 90% usage, 13F similarity) is attributed to unnamed researchers; the link to alpha half-life of trend following is asserted rather than tested, and trend following may also be crowded.
Gold's fall from above $5,000 to about $4,100 is presented as a challenge to its safe-haven role without checking whether other drivers explain it.
The decoupling thesis (fragmentation lowers correlations) is stated without correlation data; the host notes how many markets to trade is an open question.
Hedge fund bond demand elasticity is 'my guess' with no evidence.
Performance data ambiguity: the S&P 500 total return statement is ambiguous in the transcript (stated +1.43% and +14.36% YTD).

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs Mark says matter: bank and dealer intermediation capital and repo conditions, who the marginal bond buyer is (hedge fund basis trades versus central banks), the term premium and stock-bond correlation, public debt and interest-cost trajectories, commodity inventories versus five-year norms and substitutability, the degree of geo-economic fragmentation (correlation matrix), earnings momentum versus discount rate, and crowding indicators such as 13F similarity. Horizons run from months (winter stock-outs) to years (commodity supercycle, regime of normal yields).
reader_inferences: (reader) The unifying theme is that trend profits come from structural frictions (limited intermediation capital, fragmentation, stock-out nonlinearity), so he argues for ex ante mapping of frictions instead of price-only analysis.

(reader) His argument that trend following has no alpha half-life is the opposite of an overfitting-based edge; it is a claim that the premium is a payment for waiting, which also implies long dry spells.
(reader) Calling the sell-off normal while warning of elastic hedge fund demand implies fair value with large two-sided tails rather than a directional bond call.
